name: Water Surface Physics Check
description: Validates water surface dynamics against fluid simulation physics — AI-generated water often violates wave propagation rules.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated video by analyzing whether water surface dynamics obey the physics of real fluid motion. AI generators struggle to reproduce the complex, physically governed behavior of water:

1. **Wave Dispersion Relation Validation**: Surface gravity waves follow the deep-water dispersion relation: ω² = gk tanh(kh), where ω is angular frequency, g = 9.81 m/s², k = 2π/λ is the wavenumber, and h is water depth. This means longer waves travel faster than shorter waves (dispersive medium). The method performs a 3D FFT (2D spatial + 1D temporal) on water surface regions to extract the spatiotemporal frequency spectrum. In real water, energy should concentrate along the dispersion curve in (kx, ky, ω) space. AI-generated water often shows: (a) non-dispersive wave propagation (all wavelengths traveling at the same speed), (b) energy at physically impossible (k, ω) combinations, or (c) wave speeds inconsistent with the apparent depth. The method computes the fraction of spectral energy within ±15% of the theoretical dispersion surface — real water achieves > 0.85, while AI-generated water typically falls below 0.60.

2. **Capillary-Gravity Wave Transition**: Waves shorter than the capillary length (λc ≈ 1.7 cm for water) are dominated by surface tension rather than gravity, and their phase speed increases with decreasing wavelength — opposite to gravity waves. The crossover wavelength is λ* = 2π√(σ/ρg) where σ = 0.073 N/m is surface tension and ρ = 998 kg/m³ is water density. The method checks whether small-scale surface ripples follow capillary dynamics: phase speed c = √(gλ/(2π) + 2πσ/(ρλ)) with a minimum at λ* ≈ 1.7 cm (cmin ≈ 0.23 m/s). AI-generated water almost never models capillary waves correctly — it typically shows only one wave regime, or the small waves appear as texture noise rather than physically propagating capillary ripples.

3. **Reflection and Refraction Coherence**: Water surfaces act as partial mirrors whose reflectivity depends on the viewing angle following Fresnel's equations: R = ½[(sin²(θi-θt)/sin²(θi+θt)) + (tan²(θi-θt)/tan²(θi+θt))], where θt = arcsin(sin(θi)/1.33) (Snell's law with water's refractive index n = 1.33). At normal incidence, reflectivity is only ~2%, increasing to 100% at grazing angles. The method validates: (a) reflected images should distort according to the local surface normal (which changes with waves), (b) refracted underwater objects should shift position according to Snell's law, (c) total internal reflection should occur for underwater-to-air angles > 48.6° (critical angle). AI-generated water frequently shows: reflections that don't match the wave geometry, underwater objects visible at physically impossible angles, or uniform reflectivity regardless of viewing angle.

4. **Temporal Flow Coherence and Conservation**: Water is an incompressible fluid — the velocity field must satisfy ∇·v = 0 (divergence-free). The method tracks water surface motion using optical flow and checks: (a) the flow field should be approximately divergence-free (no sources or sinks on a flat water surface), (b) vorticity should decay over time due to viscosity (ν = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s for water), (c) wave interactions should follow interference rules — two waves meeting should superpose linearly (for small amplitudes), (d) breaking waves should only occur when wave steepness H/λ > 1/7 (the Stokes limit). AI-generated water commonly shows: flow fields with non-zero divergence (water appearing or disappearing), waves that pass through each other without interfering, or waves that break at unrealistic steepnesses.
parameters:
Spatiotemporal FFT: 3D (kx, ky, ω)
Dispersion tolerance: ±15% of theoretical curve
Capillary length: λc ≈ 1.7 cm
Refractive index: n = 1.33 (water)
Fresnel critical angle: 48.6° (total internal reflection)
Stokes breaking limit: H/λ > 1/7
Divergence tolerance: |∇·v| < 0.05
Minimum water region: 100×100 pixels
Frame rate requirement: ≥ 24 fps
Minimum duration: 2 seconds
accuracy: 80–89% accuracy detecting AI-generated water surfaces. Dispersion relation validation achieves AUC of 0.87. Capillary-gravity transition is highly discriminative (AUC 0.91) when small-scale ripples are visible. Fresnel reflection coherence provides F1-score of 0.83. Performance depends on water surface visibility and video resolution.
source: Tessendorf, J. (2001). Simulating Ocean Water. SIGGRAPH Course Notes.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated videos containing water surfaces (oceans, lakes, rivers, pools). Verifying physics consistency in CGI water effects for forensic analysis. Identifying synthetic nature footage. Quality validation of fluid simulation in film production.
strengths:
• Based on fundamental fluid dynamics physics (Navier-Stokes)
• Dispersion relation provides a strict physical constraint
• Capillary wave analysis exploits a scale humans rarely notice
• Fresnel reflection angles are precisely defined physical constants
• Multiple independent physics checks provide robust detection
limitations:
• Requires sufficiently large and visible water surface regions
• Turbulent water (rapids, waterfalls) is harder to analyze with linear wave theory
• Low-resolution video may not resolve capillary-scale waves
• Real water sometimes appears non-physical due to wind or subsurface currents
• Advanced physics-based fluid simulations may pass dispersion tests
